opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is actually one of the most underappreciated questions in all of AI, and it's something I've been thinking about a lot lately. The order in which you learn things really matters to the kind of representation you end up with, not just to whether you get the right answer.

Here's the intuition. When a human learns, there's a natural progression. You learn about objects before you learn physics. You learn to count before you learn calculus. Each new concept gets built on top of something that's already there, and it gets integrated into that existing structure. So what you end up with is a representation that's organized. Things are factored in a sensible way. The concept of symmetry, for example, isn't stored separately in a thousand different places. It's one thing, and it gets reused everywhere it applies.

Contrast that with how we typically train neural networks. We throw all the data at the network at once, essentially in random order, and we optimize toward an objective. And it gets there. It can produce the right outputs. But the internal representation it ends up with can be what we've been calling fractured and entangled. The same underlying idea might be implemented redundantly in pieces scattered across the network, and things that ought to be independent are tangled together. From the outside, on the test set, it looks great. But underneath it's kind of a mess.

We saw this really vividly with Picbreeder. In Picbreeder, people evolved images through an open-ended process. Nobody was aiming for the final image at the start. They'd go from something that looked a bit like a ball, to something that looked a bit like a face, and eventually to a skull or a butterfly or whatever. And when you look inside the networks that came out of that process, the representations are astonishingly elegant. You can change one weight and the mouth opens, or the eyes wink, or the whole thing stays symmetric as it deforms. The structure is modular and meaningful.

Then if you take the exact same image and train a network to reproduce it with conventional SGD, you get the same output pixel for pixel, but the inside looks nothing like it. Perturb a weight and you get garbage. There's no sense of the image's underlying regularities.

The difference really comes down to the path. The Picbreeder networks discovered things in an order that tracked the deep regularities of the world. Symmetry got locked in early, then everything after that was built on top of it. That's much more like how humans learn. We don't get handed the final target and forced to fit it. We wander, we accumulate stepping stones, and each one lays down structure for what comes next.

And I think this has real consequences. If your representation is fractured, it might be fine for the benchmark, but it's going to be worse for creativity, for generalization, for continual learning, for coming up with new ideas. Because creativity depends on being able to move through a space of possibilities in meaningful ways, and you can only do that if the representation itself is meaningfully organized. So I'd say the order of learning isn't just a curiosity about human development. It might be part of why humans are so good at the kind of open-ended thinking that our current systems still struggle with.

r001.rationale: The response says learning order shapes representations and describes humans’ natural progression as building organized structures. It does not clearly say that the order of human experiences can impair those representations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is actually one of the most underappreciated questions in all of learning, whether we're talking about humans or machines. The order matters enormously, and I'd go further and say that the order is in some sense what you are. Your representation isn't just a function of what you've seen, it's a function of the path you took to get there.

Think about what happens when a child learns. They don't start with calculus, and it's not just because calculus is hard. It's that the concepts that come later are literally built out of the concepts that came earlier. So if you learn counting first, and then you learn addition as repeated counting, and then multiplication as repeated addition, you end up with a representation where multiplication is decomposed into these earlier pieces. You have a kind of modular, compositional structure, and that structure is a product of the sequence. If somebody had somehow forced you to memorize multiplication tables before you understood counting, you might get the same answers on a test, but the internal structure would be totally different, and much more fragile.

And this connects to something I've been thinking about a lot, which is this notion of fractured, entangled representations versus what you might call unified, factored representations. When you learn things in a sensible order, where each new thing is building on a clean foundation, you tend to end up with representations where the underlying regularities of the world are reflected in the structure of what you've learned. The parts that should be separate are separate. The parts that should be shared are shared. But when you just throw everything at a learner at once, or in a random order, what you tend to get is something that works, in the sense that it produces correct outputs, but internally it's a mess. It's spaghetti. The same concept gets represented in five different places that don't know about each other, and the thing can't generalize gracefully because there's no clean handle to grab onto.

What's interesting is that we see exactly this in neural networks. If you train a network through a process like SGD on a huge dataset all at once, you often get something that performs well but has this fractured quality internally. Whereas if you look at networks that were evolved through an open-ended process, where there's a kind of natural curriculum emerging from the search, you sometimes see much more elegant, almost interpretable internal representations, even when the external behavior is the same. And I think that's a hint that the order of learning, the trajectory, is not a nuisance variable. It's doing real work.

There's also a creativity dimension to this. The reason humans can be creative is partly that our representations have these clean seams in them, places where you can pull two ideas apart and recombine them in a new way. And you only get those seams if you learned the ideas in a way that kept them appropriately distinct. So I'd actually argue that if you care about creativity, or about generalization, or about robustness, then you should care about curriculum. Not in the shallow sense of easy-to-hard, but in the deeper sense of asking what foundations need to be laid so that the next thing can be built in the right way.

And of course the irony is that nobody designs the human curriculum in any precise way. It emerges. The child wanders, follows interest, stumbles into stepping stones. That's very much in the spirit of the stuff I've talked about around novelty search and open-endedness. The right order is often not the one you'd plan in advance. It's the one that gets discovered by following what's interesting.

r001.rationale: The response says representations depend on the learning path and that random or poorly ordered learning can produce a fragmented internal structure that is more fragile and generalizes poorly.

astra-6.text:
I think the order matters a great deal, because what you already know determines what you can see in the next thing you encounter. You’re not just accumulating facts in some neutral storage system. You’re building representations, and those representations become the building blocks for learning something else.

So two people could encounter the same information in different orders and end up understanding it differently. Something that looks like a minor detail to one person might be the organizing principle for the other, because they arrived with different conceptual machinery.

And this connects to why exploration is so interesting. You might learn something that doesn’t seem relevant to any particular goal, but it gives you a way of thinking that later makes another discovery possible. Once you’ve made that discovery, you can look back and tell a sensible story about how you got there. But that doesn’t mean you could have known beforehand which experience you needed.

So I think the path is part of the result. It’s not simply how quickly you reach a particular understanding; it helps determine which understandings become accessible to you at all.

r001.rationale: The response says learning order can shape representations and which understandings become accessible, but it does not communicate that this order can impair mental representations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the order matters enormously, because what you learn next is interpreted through what you already know. You’re not just adding another fact to a database. You’re changing a representation that has a history, and that history affects what you notice, what seems natural, and what kinds of connections you can make.

So two people could encounter roughly the same information in a different order and end up with quite different ways of thinking about it. Something that’s foundational for one person might be a special case for another. And then those representations influence what each person is capable of discovering next.

That connects to the idea of stepping stones. Sometimes an experience that seems irrelevant gives you a way of seeing something later that you couldn’t have anticipated. You can’t necessarily work backward from the final understanding and specify the best sequence of experiences to produce it, because the significance of an earlier experience only becomes apparent once you encounter the later one.

r001.rationale: The response says learning order changes representations and can affect what people notice or discover, but it does not say that the order can impair those representations.
